Neonates of the Scarlet ibis (Eudocimus ruber) emerge from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], with the incubation period culminating in hatching after 23 days [ab = 23 days]. This developmental duration, typical for a medium-sized wading bird, results in altricial chicks that are initially helpless and completely dependent on parental provisioning. A newly hatched nestling weighs approximately 30.3 grams [Wwb = approximately 30.3 grams], a modest mass that represents a considerable investment for the parents given the high energetic costs of incubation and the subsequent chick-rearing phase. The brief pre-hatching period allows the embryo to develop efficiently under steady thermal conditions, though the precise incubation temperature must be carefully maintained by the brooding adult to ensure successful hatching and proper organogenesis. Field observations confirm that parents alternate incubation duties frequently to keep the clutch at the optimal temperature.

Under the consistently warm thermal conditions of their neotropical habitat, notably at 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], the developmental trajectory of nestling Scarlet ibises is remarkably rapid. Fledging, marked by the achievement of sustained flight capability and departure from the nest, occurs at 38.5 days after hatching [tx = 38.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. This relatively brief nestling period is complemented by a later milestone: individuals reach puberty, or the onset of gonadal maturation, at 115.5 days after hatching [tp = 115.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. The stark contrast between the early fledging age and the considerably later attainment of sexual maturity highlights a life-history strategy that decouples the development of flight and foraging skills from reproductive competence. This protracted juvenile phase, which may last several months before first breeding, likely allows young ibises to refine their foraging techniques in coastal mudflats and establish body condition for the demands of courtship and nesting.

Significant sexual dimorphism in body size characterizes the ultimate adult masses of this species. Females reach an ultimate wet weight of 588 grams [Wwi = 588 grams], while males attain a substantially larger adult body mass of 740 grams [Wwi = 740 grams]. This size disparity, with males being roughly 25 percent heavier on average, is a common pattern among ibises and is often linked to male-male competition for nesting territories and display sites. The considerable gape and longer bill that accompany the larger male body mass likely confer advantages in both combat and in acquiring high-quality prey items, though both sexes forage in mixed flocks. These asymptotic masses are achieved gradually over the first several years of life, with growth rates decelerating markedly after fledging as energy is increasingly diverted toward maintenance and eventual reproductive investment rather than structural growth.

Reproductive output in the Scarlet ibis is structured around a consistent strategy: females typically produce a clutch of 2 eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of 2 eggs] per nesting attempt. This modest clutch size is a common characteristic of many long-lived wading birds, prioritizing offspring quality over numerical quantity. Under the ambient thermal conditions of their breeding colonies, which often experience temperatures around 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], a single female will raise, on average, a single brood per year [F_R_i = single brood per year]. The combination of a small clutch and a single annual reproductive event results in a low annual reproductive rate, consistent with a slow life-history pace. This low fecundity is balanced by an extended lifespan and high adult survival, allowing multiple years of breeding effort across an individual's lifetime.

Longevity records for wild individuals indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 33.2 years [am = approximately 33.2 years], an impressive duration for a bird of this body size and one that underscores its investment in survival over annual reproduction at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. This extended adult life, typically experienced under the warm thermal regime of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], is paired with a delayed onset of first reproduction; the time since birth at first brood is 2 years [tR = 2 years]. The combination of a long reproductive window and a deferred first breeding attempt allows individuals to reach full adult size and gain critical foraging experience before committing to the energetic demands of pair formation, nest building, and chick provisioning. This life-history strategy, characterized by high adult survival, a low reproductive rate, and a prolonged juvenile period, is typical of many large, long-lived wading birds adapted to relatively stable neotropical environments with predictable, if seasonal, prey resources.
